claims.text: A hybrid free-energy workflow can integrate a machine-learned interatomic potential with sparse ab initio molecular-dynamics training data.
A strategically small set of ab initio molecular-dynamics data can adequately represent the configurations needed for solid- and liquid-state free-energy calculations.
The proposed workflow can accurately predict fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties in both solid and liquid states.
The workflow can reduce computational cost by approximately an order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The workflow can reduce computational cost by approximately an order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD.
The claimed accuracy and cost reduction can extend to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Sparse ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations should be used to train a surrogate interatomic potential.
The surrogate potential can faithfully reproduce the many-body and anharmonic interactions relevant to free energies.
The intended temperature domain is typically at least 1000 K and extends up to the melting point.
The workflow is intended to cover both solid and fluid states at pressures relevant to fusion environments.
The machine-learned potential maps limited ab initio data to a computationally inexpensive representation of interatomic interactions.
Training on a minimal set of high-fidelity trajectories enables the surrogate to capture vibrational entropy.
Training on a minimal set of high-fidelity trajectories enables the surrogate to capture anharmonic fluctuations.
Training on a minimal set of high-fidelity trajectories enables the surrogate to capture electron-vibration coupling.
Capturing these entropy and coupling effects permits efficient thermodynamic integration without extensive full ab initio molecular-dynamics sampling.
Predicted free energies should remain within experimental or high-fidelity simulation uncertainty.
Transferability to chemically complex multicomponent systems may be limited.
Effectiveness under extreme chemical disorder or outside the stated temperature and pressure range remains unestablished.

A decisive benchmark can compare solid-liquid free-energy differences, melting temperatures, entropy contributions, and computational cost against full ab initio molecular dynamics and experimental melting data.
The hypothesis is falsified if predictions fall outside accepted ab initio benchmark uncertainty or if computational cost is not reduced by at least tenfold.
